paras: The lynching of Jim Jones took place about 1:30 a.m. on August 22, 1895, when a band of about twenty-five masked men broke into the Drew County jail at Monticello, Arkansas, took out Jones, a Black prisoner, and hanged him from a tree at the edge of town. Jones was accused of killing a white man named Beltzhoover near Tillar and had shot a member of a pursuing party during a jail break five days earlier. The story ran nationally by wire, and the local weekly condemned the mob while calling Jones a confessed murderer.
Jones was held in the Drew County jail awaiting trial for the killing of a white man named Beltzhoover near Tillar, Arkansas.

On the evening of Saturday, August 17, prisoners overpowered Deputy Sheriff Walter Wilson as he brought their food, and Jones took his pistol and ran toward the western edge of town with three other Black prisoners. When Wilson, James Bennett of Dermott and Zach Curry caught up with him, Jones fired four shots and wounded Bennett in the jaw before he was disarmed and returned to jail. According to the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic's Monticello correspondent, there was "considerable talk of lynching him" that day, but "the more conservative element prevailed."

In the early hours of Thursday, August 22, the men, masked and armed, came to the jail; the Monticellonian believed they had ridden in on horseback from a distance. The jailer refused their demand for the keys, so they held him and broke the jail open with crowbars and other tools. They carried Jones to the western suburbs and hanged him from a limb, where he was found the next morning.

The Little Rock wire added that Jones "begged piteously for mercy" and was given only a short time to pray, and that his body was then "riddled with bullets" and left hanging until it was cut down later that day. The local accounts do not mention the shooting; the Monticellonian described the mob as "very quiet about their work" but "determined and very much in earnest."

The sheriff had the body buried after a coroner's inquest at which, the Monticellonian reported, nothing implicated anyone. None of the lynchers was recognized, and the Monticello dispatches reported "no clew" to the participants. Opinion in Monticello, the Monticellonian reported, held that a mob from Tillar had lynched Jones because they regarded the jail as insecure. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The first reports appeared on August 23: a short Monticello dispatch in the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic headed "Drew County Lynching," and a Little Rock wire run under headlines such as "Murderer Jones Lynched" and "A Mob's Vengeance." The wire stated as fact that Jones had "murdered" Beltzhoover, and its copies gave the mob as twenty, twenty-five or, in the Age-Herald, 250 men. Shorter items ran in weekly papers in Missouri, Tennessee, Wisconsin, Minnesota and North Dakota through the end of August, several naming him "Jim Jones" and one placing Monticello in Tennessee.

On August 30 the Monticellonian printed its own account and reprinted an Arkansas Democrat editorial calling the lynching "uncalled for" and urging that the mob be "apprehended and punished." The Monticellonian agreed it was wrong to mob Jones but predicted that the mob "will never be punished," since hanging was the lawful penalty for his alleged crime. Its editor called Jones a "selfconfessed murderer" whose guilt was not in question, yet wrote that "it was wrong for the mob to take the law into their own hands."

The Monticellonian dated the jail break Saturday, August 17, and counted four escaped prisoners, while the Graphic's August 19 dispatch counted six and later dispatches said Jones broke jail "last Monday." The local paper named the accused "W. A. Jones" and his alleged victim Harry Beltzhoover, killed in September 1894, where the wire gave Jones and Whitman Beltzhoover. The Arkansas Democrat's statement that Jones "had killed two men" is not supported by the Monticellonian, which described Bennett's wound as a flesh wound from which he would soon recover.

bases: About twenty-five masked men broke into the Drew County jail, took out a Black prisoner held on a murder charge and hanged him (A5, A22, A26).

A masked band of about twenty to twenty-five men took Jones from jail against the jailer's refusal and hanged him (A22, A26, A5); he was held on a murder accusation, and the local paper called the act unlawful (A24, A23).
The local Monticellonian (A22, A26), a Pine Bluff Monticello dispatch (A5) and the Little Rock wire (A6) independently agree on the jail break-in and hanging.

accounts.label: Monticellonian (local weekly)
accounts.gist: About 25 masked, armed men held the jailer, broke the jail open with crowbars and hanged W. A. Jones to a limb in the western suburbs; the town believed a Tillar mob did it because the jail was insecure, and the inquest implicated no one.

accounts.label: Monticello dispatch (Pine Bluff Graphic)
accounts.gist: Twenty-five masked men broke the jail door down at 1:30 a.m. and took Jones, who was found hanging from a tree; no clew to the participants.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire
accounts.gist: The mob could not get the keys from Jailer Wilson and broke in; Jones begged for mercy, was given a short time to pray, was hanged, and his body was riddled with bullets and left until cut down.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Murderer Jones Lynched' and 'A Mob's Vengeance'; the wire treats the murder as established and calls Bennett 'a prominent young man'.
The Monticellonian called Jones a 'selfconfessed murderer' but said the mob had no excuse, and reprinted the Arkansas Democrat's call to punish the lynchers while predicting they never would be.
National news digests gave a one-line item, 'A masked mob ... secured Jim Jones, a negro charged with murder, and hanged him'.
